---
title: "Should we roll out the one-page checkout?"
output: github_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
r <- readRDS("reports/results.rds")
pct <- function(v, d = 1) paste0(format(round(100 * v, d), nsmall = d), "%")
pp <- function(v, d = 2) paste0(format(round(100 * v, d), nsmall = d), " pp")
eur <- function(v, d = 2) paste0("€", format(round(v, d), nsmall = d, big.mark = ","))
num <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")
p_txt <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste0("p = ", format(round(p, 3), nsmall = 3))
mobile <- r$segments[r$segments$segment == "mobile", ]
desktop <- r$segments[r$segments$segment == "desktop", ]
fp <- r$peeking$summary$false_positive_rate
monthly_gain <- r$mobile_rpv$diff * r$monthly_visitors * r$mobile_share
```

## Recommendation

Roll out the one-page checkout **on mobile**, and keep the current checkout on
desktop until a desktop test shows a benefit. On mobile, conversion rose by
`r pp(mobile$diff_median)` (95% interval `r pp(mobile$diff_low)` to
`r pp(mobile$diff_high)`). On desktop the effect is indistinguishable from zero.

## The test

The test compared the current checkout (A) with a one-page checkout (B). It ran for
14 days with `r num(r$n_visitors)` visitors split 50/50 at random. Before the
start, a power analysis fixed the sample size: detecting a lift of
`r pp(r$design$mde)` from a `r pct(r$design$base_rate)` baseline with 80% power
needs `r num(r$design$n_per_arm)` visitors per arm.

**Can the data be trusted?** The split was `r num(r$srm$counts[1])` to
`r num(r$srm$counts[2])` (sample ratio check `r p_txt(r$srm$p_value)`, so
randomisation worked). Device mix, customer mix and pre-test spend are balanced
across arms.

## Results

| Metric | A | B | B minus A (95% interval) | p-value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Conversion rate (primary) | `r pct(r$primary$rate_a, 2)` | `r pct(r$primary$rate_b, 2)` | `r pp(r$primary$diff)` (`r pp(r$primary$ci_low)` to `r pp(r$primary$ci_high)`) | `r format(signif(r$primary$p_value, 2))` |
| Revenue per visitor | `r eur(r$rpv$mean_a)` | `r eur(r$rpv$mean_b)` | `r eur(r$rpv$diff)` (`r eur(r$rpv$ci_low)` to `r eur(r$rpv$ci_high)`) | `r format(signif(r$rpv$p_value, 2))` |
| Revenue per visitor, CUPED | | | `r eur(r$rpv_cuped$diff)` (`r eur(r$rpv_cuped$ci_low)` to `r eur(r$rpv_cuped$ci_high)`) | `r format(signif(r$rpv_cuped$p_value, 2))` |
| Average order value (guardrail) | `r eur(r$aov$mean_a)` | `r eur(r$aov$mean_b)` | `r eur(r$aov$diff)` (`r eur(r$aov$ci_low)` to `r eur(r$aov$ci_high)`) | `r format(signif(r$aov$p_value, 2))` |

Conversion rose by `r pct(r$primary$relative_lift)` relative to A. The Bayesian
model puts the probability that B converts better at
`r pct(r$bayes$prob_b_better)`; the expected loss from choosing B if it is in fact
worse is `r pp(r$bayes$expected_loss_b, 4)`.

Buyers in B spend `r eur(-r$aov$diff)` less per order. The checkout wins extra
buyers with smaller baskets. Revenue per visitor still rises, but its interval is
wide because most visitors spend nothing. Adjusting for each visitor's spend in
the 30 days before the test (CUPED) narrows the interval and is equivalent to
`r pct(r$variance_reduction, 0)` less variance.

## Where the effect comes from

![](figures/segment_effects.png)

A Bayesian logistic regression (rstanarm) estimates the effect separately for
each segment. On mobile the effect is clearly positive (probability
`r pct(mobile$prob_positive)` that it is above zero). On desktop the interval
spans zero (`r pp(desktop$diff_low)` to `r pp(desktop$diff_high)`).

## Why the test ran its full length

![](figures/peeking.png)

In 2,000 simulated tests with no true difference, looking once at the planned end
declared a false winner `r pct(fp[1])` of the time, as promised. Looking every
day and stopping at the first p < 0.05 declared a false winner `r pct(fp[2])` of
the time. The test was therefore read once, after 14 days.

## What it is worth

At about `r num(r$monthly_visitors)` visitors a month, of whom
`r pct(r$mobile_share, 0)` are on mobile, the mobile revenue gain of
`r eur(r$mobile_rpv$diff)` per visitor is worth roughly
`r eur(monthly_gain, 0)` a month (95% interval
`r eur(r$mobile_rpv$ci_low * r$monthly_visitors * r$mobile_share, 0)` to
`r eur(r$mobile_rpv$ci_high * r$monthly_visitors * r$mobile_share, 0)`).

## Caveats

- The data are simulated with known effects, so the analysis can be checked
  against the truth; the effect sizes are illustrative.
- The segment comparison is exploratory. Desktop should get its own, properly
  powered test before any rollout there.
- Two weeks cannot show long-term effects such as repeat purchases or returns.
